content.summary_of_the_paper: Large-scale language models have demonstrated impressive performance in text generation and classification. However, these models lack transparency and have unpredictable blind spots and exhibit subhuman performance in certain areas. This has lead to an increased focus on salience in natural language. In this paper, the authors propose a method that only captures the signal of the later layers of the transformer stack and projects it back onto the token space of natural language.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. An adapted gradient-based saliency method is presented, which can be paired with any layer-based saliency metric, explicitly accounting for multiple layers of self-attention mechanisms and reflecting complex pre-training and task specific fine-tuning on the layers in the architecture.
2. The method is computationally-efficient and does not require additional training or labels. Moreover, the method prioritizes task-specific information over language structure.
3. Overall, an interesting method is proposed for learning saliency in NLP classification tasks.

Weaknesses:
1. The assumptions for the proposed algorithm are unclear and unrealistic. First, the equivalence between the problem of projecting scores into a token space and that of projecting outputs into a token space is not clearly explained. Secondly, the outputs of a transformer block might not be able to approximate to a weighted combination of its inputs, since an activation function (ReLU or GELU) is used in a transformer block.
2. While the MLM head is trained on the output tokens of the last layer ℎ_𝐿, the MLM head in the algorithm is now fed with the output tokens of the intermediate layer ℎ_𝑙. This design seems inconsistent and unclear to me.
3. Although the authors claim that the method is computationally efficient, no experiments demonstrate this advantage.
4. The notations are quite unclear and confusing (some are undefined), which make one very hard to understand the details of the proposedmethod. 
- What’s the difference between “T” in section 2.2 and “n”?
- Does ℎ_𝑙^𝑘 mean the k-th row or the k-th column?
- The description of 𝐷 ̂_𝑙 is unclear
5. A number of grammar mistakes or typo can be found:
- 𝑒^((𝑗)) is a 1×𝑉 basic vector with a one in column 𝑗 and “a zero” elsewhere representing… (section 2.2)
- We show “psuedocode” for our approach… (section 2.2)
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Please see my comments above. The clarity, novelty, and quality of this work are not sufficient.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper presents a strategy for identifying textual saliency in large-scale language models applied to classification tasks. The authors adapt gradient-based saliency methods for transformer-based networks, and propose a method for evaluating the degree of semantic coherence of each layer, demonstrating consistent improvement over numerous other methods for textual saliency on multiple benchmark classification datasets. The proposed approach requires no additional training or access to labelled data, and is comparatively very computationally efficient. However, as pointed out in the weakness, the technical details and presentation of this work still require significant improvements.

content.title: Response to Reviewer UMGB
content.comment:
We would like to thank Reviewer UMGB for providing a detailed review and we have worked to improve the presentation and clarity of the work in response to the comments. We have repasted the questions in _italics_ and addressed them individually after each question. We have also uploaded a revised version of the paper with all the suggested changes.

Additionally, we would also like to ask for clarity on your review of the paper's novelty; none of your comments mention it, yet you confidently rated our paper as only marginally empirically/technically novel. Fundamentally, our approach empirically demonstrates state of the art performance on benchmark datasets without computationally-expensive probing for decision boundaries that other high-performing approaches use. It's widely applicable, makes minimal assumptions, and provides insight into heretofore unexplored layers of one of the more powerful and popular NLP architectures. We believe that this power, flexibility and utility merits a higher score, and hope you will consider it.

1. _The assumptions for the proposed algorithm are unclear and unrealistic. First, the equivalence between the problem of projecting scores into a token space and that of projecting outputs into a token space is not clearly explained. Secondly, the outputs of a transformer block might not be able to approximate to a weighted combination of its inputs, since an activation function (ReLU or GELU) is used in a transformer block._

By definition, the indices of a score vector for a layer and the indices of the output vector for the same layer are the same. Thus if the $i-th$ element of the output vector projects into token space onto the axes representing tokens A, B and E, then its feature values are composed of contributions from tokens A, B and E. Similarly the $i-th$ element of the score vector, which has the same indices, has a score value that is going to be composed of contributions from the same tokens A, B and E.

ReLU functions are piecewise linear and thus we do not believe this to affect the projections. This is supported in our experimental results; however, it could be interesting future work to have a theoretical paper on this.

2. _While the MLM head is trained on the output tokens of the last layer_ _ℎ __\___ 𝐿 __, the MLM head in the algorithm is now fed with the output tokens of the intermediate layer_ _ℎ__ \ ___𝑙__. This design seems inconsistent and unclear to me._

As argued in the second paragraph of page 5, we conjecture that because the pre-training tasks are performed over an enormous corpus (Wikipedia etc.), the learned function $f^lm(·)$ is estimating the map between $\mathbb{R}^K$ and $\mathcal{T}$. In other words, while $f^lm(·)$ is trained to learn the connection between $h\_L$ and their corresponding tokens, the corpus it is trained on is so large, it fills the entire function space $\mathbb{R}^K$ and thus $f^lm(·)$ is learning the connection between the entire space and the corresponding token space. This is why we believe we can use $f^lm(·)$ as a universal decoder for any output layer $h\_l$ as they all lie in the feature space $\mathbb{R}^K$. This could also be interesting future work for a theoretical paper to attempt to prove this conjecture.

3. _Although the authors claim that the method is computationally efficient, no experiments demonstrate this advantage._

As mentioned in your comments in the "Strengths" section, our method does not require any additional training or labels. That is what we mean by computationally efficient. We can "time" our method, but the only real computational costs are a backward pass to a certain layer and a forward "prediction" to the token space. Furthermore, we don't have a comparison to "time" against in experiments because as mentioned in Feldhus et al. (2021), many of their explainers are computationally challenging and the purpose of their Thermostat package is to circumvents redundant computations and increases comparability and replicability.

content.title: Response to Reviewer UMGB Continued
content.comment:
4. _The notations are quite unclear and confusing (some are undefined), which make one very hard to understand the details of the proposed method._

- _What's the difference between "T" in section 2.2 and "n"?_

$T$ is described in the paragraph above Equation (5) as a subset of $V$ that correspond to the unique tokens in the input sequence. $n$ is the length of the input sequence and the number of rows $h\_l$ or $\hat{P}\_{l}$, but these rows do not correspond to tokens except in the 0-th layer. The reason why they do not correspond except in the 0-th layer is discussed at the end of Section 2.1.

- _The description of_ _𝐷 __ ̂\___ 𝑙_ _is unclear_

We noticed a typo where we incorrectly said $\hat{D}\_{l}$ is a $n \times T$ matrix, but it should be a $T \times n$ matrix. The rows of $\hat{D}\_{l}$ are the subset-ed columns of $\hat{P}\_{l}$ corresponding to the unique tokens in the input sequence as explicitly defined in Line 5 of Algorithm 1. We have also attempted to make the notation more clear and consistent between Algorithm 1 and the rest of the paper so that $i$ always refers to rows and $j$ always refers to columns.

- _Does_ _ℎ __\___ 𝑙 __^__ 𝑘_ _mean the k-th row or the k-th column?_

$k$ are the columns of $h\_l$ that correspond to the $K$ features of the output sequence. We have clarified this in the description after Equation (1).

5. _A number of grammar mistakes or typo can be found:_

- 𝑒_^(( __𝑗__ )) is a 1×__𝑉_ _basic vector with a one in column_ _𝑗_ _and "a zero" elsewhere representing… (section 2.2)_

We have fixed this typo, thank you!

- _We show "psuedocode" for our approach… (section 2.2)_

We have fixed this typo. Thanks.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes to explain which input token is important (salient) to a language model for making a decision, based on the interpretability method widely used in computer vision, Grad-CAM. A language model head is learned to build the connection between the input space and a specific embedding space(layer), Eq.(2). The language model is actually a weighted sum of one-hot word vectors, as shown in Eq.(3). The explainability problem of self-attention mechanism is solved by the decomposition in Eq.(4), which was previously studied in other works. The learned model can detect which input tokens are more salient to a classification task. The effectiveness of the method has been validated on the tasks of hiding/revealing games and token overlap.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength: 1. This method can overcome the entanglement of tokens when interpreting a transformer model.  2. This proposed method relies on investigation on the learned model weight, which is more efficient than black-box explainers by tweaking the input. 3. This method can be applied to a specific layer in a pre-trained model for interpretability, not necessarily to go through all of the blocks. Which can be better utilized to understand models layer-wise.

Weaknesses: 1. This study briefly discussed about the features learned by different layers of a transformer based on [Rogers et al. (2020)], however, I did not see any related discussion in the experiment section. More details can be added to explain why layer 7 performs the best on the SST-2 dataset, Table 1. 2. From Table 2, layer 6 performs as well as "Shapely" on the AG dataset for revealing, but "Shapely" is a lot better for hiding, some discussion can be added to explain potential limitations of the proposed method, do those methods focus on different aspects?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The overall writing of the draft is satisfying. Although some of the tricks are from previous studies, I believe there is moderate novelty in this paper.
content.summary_of_the_review: I admit that I have limited background in NLP, so I might miss some important issues in that area. Nevertheless, the overall idea seems plausible, using Grad-CAM like methods to interpret salient input tokens, and applying Eq.(4)(from other studies) to disentangle the attention mechanism. I would recommend this draft as weak accept.

content.title: Response to Reviewer CACK
content.comment:
We would like to sincerely thank Reviewer CACK for providing a detailed review with insightful questions. We have repasted the questions in _italics_ and addressed them individually after each question. We have also uploaded a revised version of the paper with all the suggested changes.

_1. This study briefly discussed about the features learned by different layers of a transformer based on [Rogers et al. (2020)], however, I did not see any related discussion in the experiment section._

_More details can be added to explain why layer 7 performs the best on the SST-2 dataset, Table 1._

We have added a bit of discussion in the paragraph above Tables 1 and 2. For convenience we have also pasted it below

"Another noteworthy observation is that our best performing layers (5-8 for the SST-2 dataset and 6,8 and 9 for the AG News dataset) roughly correspond to the "middle layers" described by \cite{rogers2020primer}. Thus our saliency method is only including information downstream from these layers, namely those corresponding to the "final layers", which are described to be more task-specific."

While our results show that the ordering of the best or most "useful" layers is roughly in-line with the conclusions from Rogers et al. (2020), we cannot comment on specifically why say layer 7 performs better than layer 6 as we are not studying the importance of specific layers. Furthermore, it is very possible that while generalizations about the role of specific sections of the architecture (e.g. first, middle, last) can be made, there is too much noise and dataset specificity to make generalizations about the role of specific layers.

_2. From Table 2, layer 6 performs as well as "Shapely" on the AG dataset for revealing, but "Shapely" is a lot better for hiding, some discussion can be added to explain potential limitations of the proposed method, do those methods focus on different aspects?_

Shapely along with a couple of the other Thermostat explainers is specifically trained to find perturbations that change the class of the prediction. Thus it is designed to "win" at the Hiding Game. We do not find it a limitation that our model does not focus on this for two reasons:

1. It is extremely computationally expensive to train a model to probe for perturbations that cause changes in the prediction. Both because it requires additional training and because of the combinatorial expense. Thermostat also provides two other explainers (DeepLiftShapely and GradientShapely) that circumvent the combinatorial expense by approximating the Shapely SHAP values, but also do not perform nearly as well.
2. Finding perturbations of tokens that change the prediction does not necessarily imply explainability as argued in our experiments in Section 3.2. It can be possible to find token perturbations that create enough noise to distort the classifier's decision and produce a different decision because the token perturbation is creating an out of distribution effect, which is specifically explored in Hase et al. (2021).
